rationale: Coloured on-screen display of remembered scenes via spectroscope points toward showing mental imagery, but the quote only describes colours and a glowing girl, with no brain decoding like the fMRI reconstruction.
The speaker's certainty that the computer knows what it talks about suggests an expert oracle, but nothing says it answers natural-language factual questions as START did.
Speaking name, number and rating into a machine that responds matches voice input to a terminal; the mechanism is unstated and the output is a metal disc.
A robot attendant poised to take drinks orders matches robot waiters taking diners' orders; how it works is not described and the setting is a spaceship.
A million-plug board ringing a tank evokes a big central situational display loosely, but the quote shows no computer or real-time data feed like SAGE.
Energy-beings that out-compute calculators are creatures, not a machine answering questions in language, so this does not match START.
A metallic robot-receptionist voice points toward a robot serving the public but gives no task beyond speaking; it is a thin match to a robot waiter taking orders.
A giant cybernetics machine filling the U.N. building is a central machine, but the quote alone does not say it directs robots, unlike the Volvo carrier fleet.
Naming fingerprint and retinal patterns as identity checks matches retinal scanning for identification, though no machine operation or access control is described.
Oiling a humanoid casino robot is about its maintenance and looks; it shows no service task like taking orders.
Putting a cylinder in an index system and knowing everything about a person in two minutes matches remote database retrieval; the mechanism and the interplanetary scale differ.
A brain-attached device recording tastes for conformity is neuro-surveillance, not credit scoring or computerized consumer analytics.
Looking up a planet in a Galactic Directory matches querying an online database from a terminal; the quote says nothing about how it is accessed.
Business machines for illiterates handling cards and recordings do not clearly recognize speech; the quote gives no voice input.
A robot reading a held-out card with scanners and acknowledging matches machine-readable ID cards at a station; optical reading versus IBM's data collection differs in context.
A robot referee silencing a crowd is a robot in a public role, but there is no ordering or serving function, so only loosely like the restaurant robots.
Humanoid robots controlled by the computing sections of a master machine match one central computer directing many robots; they are servants, not factory carriers.
A plastic disk dropped into a slot and read by a machine that speaks matches an ID card read at a station; the voice announcement is extra.
A giant machine finding a similar picture in its files with full details matches face-to-record matching; the mechanism is unstated and there is no live capture.
A tennis robot scooting about a court is a sports opponent, not a robot taking orders or serving the public.
Uniting mind and matter is a philosophical claim with no machine reading or reconstructing mental images.
Talking into a device and having words appear on paper matches dictation transcription in function; how it works is not given.
A woman changing before his eyes is shape-shifting, with no mind decoding in the quote.
Pictures tied to an ident-card at a police bureau suggest identity matching, but the quote does not say faces are matched automatically.
A logic computer asked about its own security and failing is not a system answering factual questions in plain language.
Humanoid waiters guided by a robot brain in the basement match one central computer controlling many robots; the restaurant setting differs from AGV fleets.
Putting a captive under Scanners hints at a mind-reading device, but the quote says nothing about what is decoded.
A device that translates thoughts into spoken words matches decoding brain activity into language, but the fMRI result decoded only imagined visual patterns.
Gates recognizing a person and opening is automated recognition for access, but the quote does not say faces are used.
An automated voice asking visitors if they have an appointment is a reception role, weakly like a robot taking orders from the public.
A button press that flips a card out of a slot evokes retrieval of records, but it is mechanical and lacks the remote computer link.
Entering a code on a reference panel and getting cards from an information bank matches terminal queries to a database; a mechanical card slot is not DIALOG.
Pressing console buttons while a typer clicks out results matches a terminal querying a database and printing output.
Teleoperated radiation robots and foremen robots are remote handling, not one computer directing a robot fleet.
A language put into the subconscious and triggered by a symbol is loosely like learning in sleep, but the quote mentions no sleep or audio.
A voice-cued setter that records memos matches voice command and dictation; recognizing a spoken cue is implied but not detailed.
Controlling robots without area computers is the opposite of one computer directing many robots.
Speaking into a dictator to record a message matches dictation; the quote does not say it converts speech to text.
A robot answering instantly like a straight man has no security patrol function in the quote.
Wearing a sleep-learner while studying cybernetics matches learning during sleep; the quote gives no mechanism beyond that.
Audioscribing a report to a computer matches spoken-to-text transcription; no mechanism shown.
A machine throwing captives' thoughts onto a screen matches displaying mental content; it gives no decoding method, and it requires hypnosis.
A machine reads the mind and retranslates the readings into visual images shown to the subject, matching reconstructing imagery from brain activity; the context is a drama and the method is vague.
A mike following body heat and a canned voice is a sensor-greeter, not a robot taking orders or serving.
An interpreter that hears questions and answers from microtapes suggests speech interaction, but no recognition of spoken words is claimed clearly.
Robots obeying spoken commands match voice command in function, but the mechanism and vocabulary are not given.
Choosing a companion's cheerful, submissive traits hints at a configurable personality, but a toy like Furby is not described and the quote gives no companion function.
Floating serving-robots offering refreshments at a party match robots serving the public; they bring drinks rather than take orders, and float.
A huge three-dimensional chart of a star system is a big display, but nothing says it updates live from a computer as SAGE consoles did.
Cyber IX used as an integrator by the sciences says nothing about answering questions posed in ordinary language to the public.
An advertisement promising innermost thoughts revealed gestures at mind-reading entertainment, with no mechanism and no imagery reconstruction.
A camera feeding a police computer that alerts robots resembles a robot security network, but no patrolling robot guard like the Sentry is described.
Fitting the eye to a cup at a wall for a retinal pattern that cannot be duplicated matches retinal-scan access control closely; the guarded base context differs.
Robot bartenders mixing and serving drinks match a robot serving the public; judging drunkenness from speech goes beyond the 1985 waiters.
A wall greeting visitors and asking about appointments is an interactive speaking receptionist; the quote shows no recognition of the visitor's speech.
Machines rejecting a blacklisted card number match machines reading an ID card at a station; the denial of food is beyond time-keeping, but the card read matches.
A turnstile reading a pass and locking on a fake pass matches machine-read access cards; it also checks money, and nothing is said about recording identity.
Identification tabs bearing a psychometric number are loosely like ID cards, but nothing is said of a machine reading them at a station.
A huge tank displaying exact positions of every enemy unit matches a 3D spatial display for viewing positions; volumetric hardware is unstated and the use is tactical.
A voice prompt asking users to state their request matches voice query to a computerized information service; the answer is directing to offices, not DIALOG searches.
A hotel staffed entirely by robot servants matches robots serving the public in a commercial venue, though ordering is not described.
A robojeep reporting status to its owner is a servant robot with voice report, loosely like a service robot; it is not serving the public.
A book answering a spoken query by naming a shelf location matches a question-answering system in function; it is a library index, not a general knowledge computer.
Predicting a person's action from muscular and nervous preparation is a loose cousin of decoding brain signals, but it does not read thoughts or images.
The Answerer that answers anything is an all-knowing question machine, but START only answered limited English questions, so only the function loosely matches.
Robots turning their ears toward a commanding human voice match robots obeying spoken commands; recognition of words is implied rather than shown.
A servo-mechanism told to pick someone up is a generic mechanical helper and does not show a robot taking orders from patrons.
A colossal mechanical brain made by the best scientists is an oracle by implication, but the quote does not say it answers questions.
Making twenty-five copies at once is a duplicating feature, not conversion of speech into text.
An index in a reading room that finds what the narrator wants matches computerized retrieval from a terminal; no details of query or mechanism.
A desk secretary announcing a meeting is a speaking device, but nothing shows it hears or recognizes spoken commands.
Splitting sound into frequency bands with separate analyzers hints at the spectral analysis used in recognizers, but is for studying alien speech, not recognition.
Mechanical devices guarding against clandestine burials are a guard automaton in a vague sense, lacking patrolling security robot detail.
Redesigning receptionist robots to face the public indicates robots meeting people, but the quote describes only appearance.
A chrome-trimmed EEP gliding out to the boy is a personal robot, weakly like a toy companion, with no interaction described.
A thought-helmet used to enter an alien brain implies reading mental content, but it is telepathic and lacks any decoding mechanism.
Probing a robot's neck to disable its memory is about tampering with a doorman, not a service function such as ordering.
Barking a command into an order box matches voice command of a terminal; no recognition mechanism is described.
A building that ingests and indexes reports from all planets then files them matches a database for later retrieval; querying is not shown here.
Maizie as a maternal figure magnified is a metaphor and the quote does not say that it answers questions.
Directors of incredible machinery whom he must stop point at remote control of many machines, but they are humans and no computer is named.
A robot sliding up and scanning his features in an establishment matches an automated patrol/checking robot; face recognition is only implied.
A wall arm restraining a person is a security robot, but the quote shows no patrol, so only loosely like a Sentry.
The ship's big computer is a shipboard computer, which loosely resembles an onboard computer running a station; the quote does not say it controls the craft.
A voice-writer producing clear script matches speech converted to text; the mechanism is not described.
A fat man in dark glasses, from the quote alone, is not a robot police device; nothing relevant to the milestone.
A master intelligence in tune with every robot on its own wavelength matches one central computer directing many robots; scale is continental and wireless.
A current transformed into a visible representation of the thinker's thoughts matches displaying mental content from brain signals; no decoding method is described.
A pineal-gland analogue contacting a chosen operator is telepathic communication with a machine, not reading thoughts out of a person.
A robot attendant wheeling a vehicle onto an elevator is a robot with a service job, but it handles cars, not people.
A head apparatus collecting thought vibrations and reproducing them matches reading brain activity to reproduce thoughts; fMRI decoded only imagined visual patterns.
A master robot commanding lesser automatons matches central control of many robots, but they explore planets and are teleoperated.
Talking at a Speak-a-Type whose keys rattle to keep up is spoken dictation turned into typed text, matching function and a sense of mechanism; the typewriter is mechanical and the context is play.
A tank spreading the exact disposition of every enemy unit matches a live situation display of tracked units; no computer processing is shown.
A ponderous wheeled vehicle rolling toward two people says nothing about patrolling or guarding, so it does not match the Sentry.
Sleek winged silver robots describe only appearance, not a computer directing a fleet.
A robot made to give pleasure and carrying memorized erotica is a companion idea in the right direction, but a Furby is a toy with no such function.
An application sent downstairs for the big computer to process is a loose pointer at computer-based record lookup, with no query terminal described.
A machine draining a sleeper's knowledge each night is a mind-extraction idea, but there is no image decoding and the method is alien.
A world map and space map with coloured pictorial symbols resemble command displays, but nothing says they update from a computer.
Gold-plated robot pages gliding to carry messages are service robots, but in a chamber, not serving the public by taking orders.
A lock actuated by light rays with a held combination is a non-card access mechanism, lacking any identity reading as in the IBM 357.
An auto-learner that planted words in the mind during training is a learning device, but the quote does not mention sleep or memory associations.
A prompt telling users to say 'Publications' implies words recognized from speech; it is a small-vocabulary command, as in 1972 recognizers, but the mechanism is not shown.
A memory bank of all human knowledge that scans and predicts is an oracle, but the quote has no question answering for the public.
Saying 'first' to an elevator, which then acts, is a single-word voice command, close to isolated-word recognition; the context is an elevator, not industrial terminals.
A street kiosk information robot that answers people matches a robot serving the public; it answers questions rather than taking food orders.
A table-map where red circles automatically show positions of air-cities matches a live automated situation display, but no computer is mentioned.
A door that rises at her voice matches voice command of a machine; no recognition mechanism is described.
A master wristband that opens a door matches an identity device read by a door; the card is a wristband and no recording takes place.
A mechanical doll as a lovely and undemanding woman is a companion robot in a loose sense, but no toy interaction is described.
Mechanical mixers in high-class joints suggest drink-mixing machines, which is a small step toward robot serving, but no robot service role.
Thought images thrown on a screen from a living subject match displaying mental imagery; the fMRI work decoded only simple patterns and the screen method differs.
A robot dealer announcing a game is a robot in a public job, weakly related to waiter robots taking orders.
A triggered electronic key opening airlocks is an access token, but there is no reading of an identity card at a station.
A keyed number combination that makes arms look up words resembles a mechanized lookup, but it is a dictionary, not a computer retrieval system.
A robot attendant offering help is a speaking helper, only weakly like robot waiters.
A power machine with a cybernetic brain that controls creatures loosely hints at central control of machines, with no description of a fleet.
A local machine referring queries to a master System Computer suggests networked query handling, but it gives no answer at all.

Turning on a vocoder and telling the Cow to supply a recording matches speaking commands to a computer; recognition is implied.

Storage banks reveal the object to be a gun by looking up stored data, which is a loose retrieval idea with no terminal.
Being deep-probed implies extracting information from the brain by machine, but the quote gives no output form such as images.
Searching the Archives for information on a person points to records lookup, but the mechanism is unspecified.
Recorded behavior analyzed by a computer and used to brief robot guards is predictive analytics with no patrolling robot.
Robot guards passing a man only after being shown an ident card match a robot guard checking IDs; the Sentry patrolled and did not check cards.
Reading the brains of the recently dead is mind reading by gist, without images or any scanner method.
A table voice that announces the menu and answers a spoken order matches voice ordering of food; recognition is implied, not described.
A building that takes in and files news by category matches an indexed database, though querying is not covered here.
Central Intelligence as a creator of perfect plans only loosely suggests a controlling machine, with no mention of directing robots.
An indexograph reporting a man's character reads like a character detector, but the quote has no thought imagery.
Directing the Cow through a vocoder panel to take over controls matches spoken commands to a computer; recognition is implied.
A glowing three-dimensional panorama of the Solar System matches a 3D display in function; the method is not stated and radiation planning is a different use.
Conceiving a means to turn the spoken word directly into print states the exact function of dictation transcription; it is only a stated goal with no mechanism.
The Brain controlling the Hive is hinted at, but this fragment does not mention robots or how they are directed.
A door's say-who-please prompt answered by speaking a name matches voice-input identification of a short utterance; how the system recognizes the speaker is not given.
Photographing retinas for the blood-vessel pattern matches retinal biometric capture; here it serves impersonation and not an access check.
A cylinder that seizes and floods the mind with green fire is a telepathic assault with no readout of brain activity.
Articles written on a voco-typer for magazines show a speaking-to-write machine in routine use; the quote gives no mechanism.
Automatons anyone can buy for a few shares are a purchasable artificial companion, but the quote says nothing of interaction or toy form.

A mechanical brain assembling information on demand, for a time, matches a computer retrieval of data; no terminal or query language is described.
Robots with long arms or truck bodies describe specialized machine shapes, not any central control.

A space-chart where ship-dots move toward glowing circles matches a live display of fleet positions; whether a computer drives it is not said.
Super-electronic gadgets sensitive to thought-waves point at a thought-detecting machine, but the quote offers no decoding or output.
A stereoscopic star chart on film showing a wedge of space is a 3D visual, but it is a viewed image, not a display of a volume.
A brain-reader that produced the narrator's tale suggests extracting thoughts from the unconscious mind, but there is no method or imagery.

A raised table-map with red circles for air-cities is a map display; the quote does not say it is three-dimensional or computer-driven.
Black cubes that are subliminal instructors give a form of teaching, but the quote does not say they work during sleep.
